correctness.rationale: For every zero-mass signed measure, its product metric distance profile is the sum of the factor distance profiles of its coordinate marginals. The exact identity half-oscillation(sum_i profile_i) = sum_i half-oscillation(profile_i) holds because coordinates of the complete Cartesian product vary independently. A coordinate-line lift makes the marginal map surjective, so the induced quotient is precisely the l1 direct sum; rank-nullity gives kernel dimension. Equilateral factor profiles are -lambda times the marginal, yielding centered oscillation norms. Their exact vertex characterization by two-level cuts and q(q-1) irredundant ordered-pair facet inequalities gives the Hamming face counts through standard l1-sum polarity. The interaction rectangle proves non-normativity for at least two factors. Eight rational finite-product tests independently verified the norm identity and rank identity; exact inequality-enumeration recovered q=2,3,4,5 factor vertex sets. These checks are not used as infinite proofs.

originality.rationale: The 2008 definition of the double-point seminorm and the 2019 paper’s isolated kernel examples are acknowledged, not relabeled. Inspected full texts do not provide the complete factor-marginal norm identity or its canonical isometric l1-direct-sum quotient for arbitrary finite sum-metric factors, nor the weighted Hamming quotient facet/vertex formulas. Known Cartesian distance-matrix identities are explicitly excluded as an independent novelty assertion. Actual searches for double-point product/Hamming/tensorization variants and mathematical records yielded no matching stronger result. The relevant 2019 distance-matrix paper was only available at abstract level, leaving disclosed residual bibliographic risk; negative search results are not treated as uniqueness proof.
residual_risks: The full text of Bapat and Kurata (2019) was not available; it may contain additional relevant algebraic comparisons beyond its abstract, but its described scope is matrix rank and inverse rather than Banach norm geometry.
A differently named or unindexed discussion of double-point product quotients could exist; search absence does not certify uniqueness.
The elementary factor polytope vertex/facet counts are classical as stand-alone convex geometry; originality attaches to their exact identification as double-point quotients.

value.rationale: The double-point seminorm was introduced as a natural compatible alternative to transport cost, yet its kernel can be nontrivial. The theorem supplies a complete, canonical description on every finite sum-metric Cartesian product, separating surviving one-coordinate marginals from entirely invisible multi-coordinate interactions. On weighted Hamming spaces, where ordinary transportation geometry grows in ambient dimension product_i(q_i)-1, it computes the exact much-smaller quotient, a closed vertex/facet census, and the sharp threshold where double-point normativity fails. These are natural structural and facial invariants of a motivated Banach quotient, not an arbitrary fixed numerical slice. The formula can be useful to compare alternative compatible metrics and to build exact finite-dimensional quotient examples. It does not claim novelty for abstract root-polytope counts outside the double-point identification.
